I am 64 years old and have farmed in Quzhou County all my life. I never went to school — my father needed my hands in the field when I was young — but I know this land better than any book ever could. My wife and I have 8 mu of good flat land here on the North China Plain, and I will farm it the same way I have for over forty years.

It is spring now, and my wheat is already in the ground. I sowed it last October, right after the autumn harvest, using luyuan502 — an improved variety that my neighbors and I have trusted for a long time. I saved some seed from last year and bought the rest from the shop in town. The wheat is greening up now, and it needs my care. I will irrigate it four times before the June harvest — our well water is reliable, and winter wheat cannot go thirsty in the dry spring. I put down urea and some compound fertilizer at the base, and I will topdress again when the wheat starts to joint. I use the rotary tiller before sowing to break up the soil and mix in the straw. Pests and weeds are a constant battle, so I will spray four times — insecticide, herbicide, and fungicide when the weather turns damp. I expect about 500 kilograms per mu if the weather is kind.

After we cut the wheat in early June, I will plant maize immediately on the same land. I always buy denghai605 hybrid seeds in bags from the dealer — they cost more, but the yield is good and the grain buyers know the variety. I do not till the land for maize; I sow directly into the wheat stubble. It saves diesel, saves my old back, and keeps the moisture in the soil. Maize is simpler than wheat. I will irrigate twice during the summer if the rains are light, and spray three times for insects and weeds. By October, I should harvest about 550 kilograms per mu of maize.

I do not grow cotton or vegetables like some of the younger farmers — too much risk, too much labor, and my wife and I cannot manage it at our age. The wheat-maize rotation is steady. It feeds us, the grain station buys it, and I understand every part of it. I will do what I have always done.

decision.reasoning_summary: I stick to the wheat-maize rotation that has fed my family for decades because it is reliable and I understand it. At 64 with no schooling, I rely on experience, neighbor knowledge, and what the local shop sells. I use improved wheat seeds saved from last year and bought hybrid maize seeds for strong yields. I till with the rotary tiller for wheat but sow maize no-till into wheat stubble to save labor and moisture. Fertilizer means urea and compound — heavy on nitrogen because that is what pushes yield on this plain. I irrigate when the crop looks thirsty and spray when I see pests or weeds. I do not gamble on new crops; I do what works.
